procedural_history.impugned_order: Order for the detention of the petitioner made by the District Magistrate on February 10, 1971, under s. 3 of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: It is mentioned that Bengal, W.P. No. 8 of 1972 decided on May 5, 1972. was followed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner, Abdus Sukkur, filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India to challenge his detention. The Supreme Court was approached because the State Government took 27 days to consider and reject the petitioner's representation against his detention, and this delay was initially unexplained in the State Government's affidavit. The Supreme Court adjourned the matter on May 5, 1972, to allow the State Government to file an additional affidavit explaining the delay.

issue.issue_text: Whether an undue and unexplained delay by the detaining authority in considering and disposing of a representation made by a detenu against a preventive detention order violates the constitutional right guaranteed under Article 22(5) of the Constitution.

facts: A petitioner, held under a preventive detention order, submitted a representation to the State Government.
The State Government took 27 days to consider and reject this representation.
The government was given an opportunity by the Court to explain this delay but failed to do so, meaning the delay was 'undue and unexplained'.
law: Article 22(5) of the Constitution guarantees that a person under preventive detention shall be afforded the 'earliest opportunity of making a representation' against the detention order.
application: The Supreme Court interpreted the right to the 'earliest opportunity' to make a representation as necessarily implying a corresponding constitutional obligation on the detaining authority to consider and dispose of that representation promptly and expeditiously.
The Court reasoned that if the authority does not act promptly, the right to make a representation is reduced to a 'farce and empty formality,' losing its purpose and meaning.
This requirement is essential because the matter concerns the personal liberty of a person detained without a regular trial, demanding strict compliance with legal procedures.
The Court cited a series of precedents where unexplained delays, some as short as 17 days, were deemed sufficient to render a detention illegal.
In this specific case, the 27-day delay by the State Government remained unexplained.
The Court held that this unexplained delay constituted an infraction of the constitutional provision.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that an undue and unexplained delay by the detaining authority in disposing of a detenu's representation violates the constitutional right guaranteed under Article 22(5). Therefore, the unexplained 27-day delay was sufficient to invalidate the petitioner's detention.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an undue and unexplained delay by the detaining authority in considering and disposing of a representation made by a detenu against a preventive detention order violates the constitutional right guaranteed under Article 22(5) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The State Government received the petitioner's representation against his detention on October 28, 1971, but only considered and rejected it on November 24, 1971, after a delay of 27 days.
This delay by the State Government was unexplained.
The constitutional right under Article 22(5) to make a representation implies that it must be considered promptly and expeditiously by the government.
An unexplained delay in considering the representation is an infraction of the constitutional provision, as it pertains to the personal liberty of a person detained without a regular trial.
Such a delay renders the detention invalid.
respondent_arguments: The State offered no explanation for the delay, stating that no additional affidavit would be filed to justify the time taken to consider the representation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The constitutional right to make a representation against a preventive detention order under Article 22(5) necessarily implies that the appropriate authority is bound to consider and dispose of the representation as expeditiously as possible. An undue or unexplained delay by the authority in dealing with the representation constitutes an infraction of Article 22(5) and renders the detention invalid.
obiter: The reason for immediate consideration of the representation is that the personal liberty of a person is at stake.
The right to make a representation would be reduced to a farce and an empty formality if the authority does not pay prompt attention to it.
No definite time can be laid down within which a representation of a detenu should be dealt with, except that it must be considered as expeditiously as possible.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The constitutional right under Article 22(5) to be afforded the "earliest opportunity of making a representation" against a preventive detention order necessarily implies that the representation must be considered and dealt with promptly by the detaining authority. The requirement to provide an opportunity to make a representation would be reduced to a "farce and empty formality" if the authority, after receiving it, pays no prompt attention to it. Therefore, an undue or unexplained delay by the authority in disposing of the representation introduces a serious infirmity in the detention, rendering it invalid for being in violation of Article 22(5).
legal_tests_applied: Whether there was an undue or unexplained delay on the part of the detaining authority in disposing of the representation made by the detenu against the detention order.
why_respondent_won: The State Government received the petitioner's representation on October 28, 1971, but did not consider and reject it until November 24, 1971, resulting in a delay of 27 days.
The State Government was guilty of an unexplained delay, as it offered no justification for the time taken to consider the representation.
This undue and unexplained delay in considering the representation constitutes an infraction of the constitutional right guaranteed to the detenu under Article 22(5).
policy_considerations: The matter relates to the liberty of a subject who has been ordered to be detained without recourse to a regular trial in a court of law.
The personal liberty of a person is at stake. Any delay would not only be an irresponsible act on the part of the appropriate authority but also unconstitutional.
It is imperative that when the liberty of a person is in peril immediate action should be taken by the relevant authorities.
The authority concerned has to proceed strictly in accordance with law and any deviation from compliance with legal requirement cannot be countenanced.
